newsitem.title: USA: Dole, Clinton begin sprint to election finish.
newsitem.headline: Dole, Clinton begin sprint to election finish.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent

President Bill Clinton and Republican Bob Dole embarked on final campaign trips on Wednesday, with Dole seeking inspiration from Abraham Lincoln and Clinton battling for Democratic control of Congress.
Both candidates left Washington, aiming to stay on the road for the final six days of the campaign until the November 5 election, after which one will return the winner.
Clinton, ahead in the polls, headed for Michigan, Colorado and Arizona to boost Democratic congressional candidates as well as his own campaign while Dole flew to Tennessee.
The Dole schedule was being worked out on a day-to-day basis, as strategists and the candidate himself tried to figure out where he could best use his time.
Dole opened his day in Washington with a short visit to the Lincoln Memorial for what he said was inspiration and a moment of silent prayer for the election just six days away.
He was inspired to tell the crowd at his first rally of the day, "We are going to win this election ... We can't afford four more years of scandal and weak leadership."
In Michigan, Clinton looked rested and relaxed as he bragged about his economic record and stressed his efforts to boost women setting up small businesses.
"We are moving in the right direction and that's a good thing," he said.

The latest Reuters tracking poll showed Clinton's lead shrinking to single digits for the first time since October 24. He led Dole by 9.8 percentage points as the number of undecided voters rose above 13 percent. But Dole's support remained stuck at 33 percent -- hardly an encouraging sign.
Reform Party candidate Ross Perot was now above the eight percent mark, having risen by three points in the past week.
The Texas billionaire scheduled an evening rally in Philadelphia and issued a press release saying he would "make a major policy announcement." Aides declined to elaborate.
Other polling organisations put Clinton's lead at between 12 and 19 points, pointing to a possible landslide.
With the presidential race seemingly a foregone conclusion, attention has switched to a tight battle for control of Congress, which the Republicans won two years ago for the first time in 40 years.

A Reuters survey of 40 political scientists around the country found that nearly two thirds thought the Republicans would hold their 53-47 majority in the Senate roughly unchanged and also keep a wafer-thin edge in the House of Representatives, where they now have a 38-seat majority.
One quarter of those surveyed thought Democrats would capture control of the House.
"It will depend on weather and turnout. Dame Fortuna will tip the balance," said Lief Carter of Colorado College in Colorado Springs.
Both Clinton and Dole have been exhorting their supporters to come out and vote. Many experts believe turnout will be relatively low after an uninspiring presidential campaign.
Polls show the struggle for Congress to be extremely close with many House Republicans who swept into office on the 1994 anti-Clinton surge now struggling for survival.
Dole has found an issue in challenging the Democrats on taking questionable campaign contributions from financial interests in Indonesia and elsewhere in Asia.
Republican Chairman Haley Barbour said Wednesday there was a "rotten stench" emanating from the White House and the Democratic Committee which came from Clinton's "flagrant violations of the law."

Clinton aides said he hoped to turn the tables on his rival with a major campaign speech, possibly on Thursday, accusing Republican House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Dole of standing in the way of campaign finance reform.
